t: Why You Need To Be Brutally Honest With Difficult Students ficult-students/
q: Difficult students don’t benefit from being coddled or having smoke blown in their ears. Yet, few teachers actually tell it like it is.
It tells students that mediocre is not only good enough, but it’s celebrated. When the standard for earning praise is down around their kneecaps, what motivation do students have to go any higher?
If they can get a pat on the back from you for minimal effort, they’ll work that knowledge to get attention whenever they need it—making them feel special, haughty even, in front of their classmates.
If the thought ever enters your mind that some of your students aren’t capable of becoming well behaved, push it aside. Because it isn’t true.
A teacher’s limiting beliefs not only deeply affect students, but they also affect what the teacher is capable of.
If you’re always honest with difficult students, they’ll learn quickly that when you praise them, they can take it to the bank.
Praise based on truth will mean something to your students. Deep inside. Where real change takes place.
x: Linsin insists teachers must reject the idea that a difficult student's current behavior is 'the best they can do,' since all students retain the capacity to change.
Dishonest praise lowers behavioral standards, implies students can't meet normal expectations, and teaches manipulation for attention.

t: How To Give A Warning That Improves Behavior https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/05/22/how-to-give-a-warning-that-improves-behavior/
q: A warning is just a warning—and nothing more. So when you give one to a student for breaking a rule, leave it at that.
A warning only works when its purpose is to allow students to fix their mistakes on their own.
You have to give trust before students will show you they’re worthy of it.

If a student breaks a rule, and you’re sure the student knows what rule was broken, then you simply write his or her name on the board, place a yellow card in the student’s designated pocket, or do whatever you do to signify a warning.
Even the most well-behaved students make mistakes once in a while. Resist the urge to look the other way when they break a rule.
When your students begin to grasp that the responsibility for breaking rules in your classroom falls firmly—and solely—in their laps, behavior will improve.

t: Should Your First Consequence Be A Warning? https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2010/05/15/should-your-first-consequence-be-a-warning/
q: I’m frequently asked whether I recommend giving a warning as a first consequence. My answer is an emphatic yes.
Mrs. Fowler often reminds her students to follow classroom rules. Predictably, they break them often.
Mr. Penn is proud of his ability to stop misbehavior in its tracks with his well-practiced “look” but has grown tired of the constant battles to get students to follow his rules.
When you have a classroom management plan that includes a warning, it takes the guesswork out of handling initial misbehavior. Student breaks rule…teacher gives warning.
Doing exactly what you say you will do builds your students’ trust in you, which makes it easier to influence behavior.
You don’t have to rely on persuasion or intimidation to stop misbehavior. You don’t have to yell, remind, glare, or use any of the other stress inducing methods.
x: A warning as the first consequence eliminates three common, stress-inducing habits: reminding, glaring, and correcting students.
He illustrates each ineffective habit with a short classroom vignette showing how reminding, glaring, and correcting leave teachers stressed and students still misbehaving.

t: How To Handle An Angry, Verbally Aggressive Student e-student/
q: Emotional outbursts, temper tantrums, yelling, lashing out. Severe misbehavior like this needs to be dealt with differently than typical rule breaking.
You must hold students who act out in anger accountable—without a doubt—but not right away. You risk escalating the problem if you immediately try to pull them aside or put them in time-out.
It’s common for teachers to place a hand on a student’s shoulder in an attempt to calm. But you don’t know what students are thinking in any given moment or what they’re capable of.
Often, it’s best not to say or do anything. If the angry student stops the behavior, simply continue on with what you were doing—for now—allowing the student time to cool off.
As soon as you are able, document the student’s behavior. Write down everything said or done and interview all students near or involved in the incident.
Unless the behavior is physically aggressive, I’m not in favor of getting the principal involved. Involving administration weakens your authority and your ability to manage your classroom.
x: Linsin outlines how teachers should respond to emotional outbursts, tantrums, and verbal aggression, distinguishing them from typical rule-breaking.
